course_description:
Environmental geochemistry covers a wide range of topics focusing on the behaviour and fate of chemical elements in the Earth's surface environment and the impacts of human activities on these systems.

The course is designed as an introduction to environmental geochemistry. The focus is on natural processes and how they connect, and interact, with anthropogenic activities in the surficial environment, affecting weathering that, in turn, drives the biogeochemical processes that occur at or near the Earth’s surface.

The course employs practical aspects of these phenomena, including laboratory exercises, e.g., the bioremediation of an oil spill and the chemistry of acid mine drainage environments associated with mining. The skills learned in this course will be applicable for students aiming for a career in the environmental sector, in the minerals industry or as a researcher in academia.

course_aims: This course is aimed at advanced undergraduate and graduate students who are interested in understanding the principles and practical aspects of applying geochemistry to natural and anthropogenic environmental investigations. It includes geochemical processes in the surficial environment; the dispersion of elements going from rock to soil; and the role of water in controlling the chemical and physical behaviour of chemical elements. The course will be classroom and laboratory focussed and will include the interpretation of geochemical data.

learning_outcomes.description: Know how to use a periodic table to combine atoms into molecules.
Know how to write and balance geochemical reactions.
Develop an understand of geochemical processes in surficial environments.
Apply the knowledge gained to real-life situations.
Working safely in a laboratory environment using geochemical reactions to design & implement chemical experiments.
Develop team building and teamwork skills during Group Work activities

You are required to submit assessable items on time. If you fail to meet the submission deadline for any assessment item, then 10% of the maximum possible mark for the assessment item (the assessment ‘marked from’ value) will be deducted as a late penalty for every day (or part day) late after the due date.
For example, if you submit your assignment 1 hour late, you will be penalised 10%; if your assignment is 24.5 hours late, you will be penalised 20% (because it is late by one 24-hour period plus part of another 24-hour period).
